【原视频简介】
Can you recover gold from old computer CPUs using traditional smelting techniques? In this experiment, I crush four ceramic CPUs, combine them with a borax-based flux and lead collector, and smelt everything down to concentrate the precious metals into a single lead button.

After separating the slag, I cupel the button at nearly 1,800°F to remove the lead and base metals, leaving behind a precious metal bead. Along the way, an unexpected piece of steel contaminates the process, creating an interesting lesson in cupellation chemistry and demonstrating how small contaminants can affect a smelt.

To verify the final result, I send the bead for XRF analysis—and the composition is not what I expected. Instead of a nearly pure gold button, the assay reveals a surprising mix of gold and silver. In the end, the four CPUs yielded just over 0.3 grams of gold, averaging roughly 0.1 gram per CPU, along with a significant amount of silver.

In this video you'll see:

Crushing and preparing ceramic CPUs
Mixing a borax, lye, and silica flux
Lead collection smelting
Separating slag from the metal button
Cupellation to remove lead and base metals
XRF analysis of the final bead
Lessons learned to improve future CPU smelts

What do you think? Where did all the silver come from? Was it in the bonding wires, the plated pins, or another component inside the CPUs? Let me know your thoughts in the comments!
